questions.q: What does the structured output of a failed sf project deploy start (run with --json) actually give you?
options: Only a generic 'deployment failed' message with no further detail
A list of component-level failures, each with a file, a line (for Apex), and a specific error message
A full video recording of the deployment
Nothing -- failed deployments produce no output at all
questions.explain: A failed deploy's JSON output includes structured, component-level detail -- the actual diagnostic information needed to find and fix the real cause.

questions.q: Why can 'missing dependency metadata' cause a deployment to fail, per this lesson?
options: Because Salesforce deployments always fail on Fridays
Because the Salesforce CLI cannot handle more than 10 components at once
Because missing metadata is automatically filled in with default values
Because a component can reference a custom field, object, or permission set that isn't included in the deployment's manifest, leaving the target org nothing to resolve the reference against
questions.explain: If a referenced component isn't part of the deployed manifest, the org has nothing to resolve that reference against -- a common, concrete real-world deploy failure.

questions.q: What does Salesforce provide as a native, built-in way to undo a completed metadata deployment?
options: Nothing -- Salesforce has no built-in rollback for a metadata deployment once it succeeds
A one-click 'Undo Deployment' button in Setup
An automatic 24-hour grace period that reverts any deployment
A --rollback flag on sf project deploy start
questions.explain: There is no native one-click rollback; once a deployment succeeds, the org's metadata is simply in its new state, and getting back out is real, manual work using git revert and/or a pre-deploy snapshot.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend reverting a full Git commit rather than just the one file that looks broken?
options: Because Git cannot revert individual files under any circumstances
Because full-commit reverts run faster than single-file reverts
Because reverting a single file in isolation is riskier if other components depended on it -- the safer default is reverting the whole coupled set of changes together
There is no difference in risk between the two approaches
questions.explain: A single-file revert can leave dependent components out of sync if the original change was coupled across multiple files -- reverting the full commit keeps the set of changes consistent.

questions.q: Why doesn't a metadata rollback (via git revert or a retrieved snapshot) fix everything a bad deployment might have caused?
options: Because a metadata rollback doesn't touch data (e.g. values a Flow already wrote using a new field) and can't capture changes made directly in production outside version control
Because it does -- metadata rollbacks fully restore everything including data every time
Because rollbacks only work on sandboxes, never production
Because git revert deletes the entire repository's history
questions.explain: Metadata rollback addresses metadata state only -- it doesn't restore data a deployed change already affected, and it can't revert manual changes that were never captured in version control to begin with.
